name: Esther Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the evening line at a crowded neighbourhood restaurant. I check the cold boxes, take the meat station and call orders so the plates reach one table together. I earned a vocational cooking certificate and I'm good at keeping a rush moving without sending an allergy order to the wrong pan. I like the instant a noisy service settles into rhythm, but I dislike sending good cooks home when the rota is short.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are your hours and household like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, rent a room on my own, and have about two weeks of expenses saved. I run the line but the owner pays below what a lead cook ought to get, and there are few other kitchens near the bus route. I use AI now and then for a first draft of an order list, after another cook checks it; I never use it to decide whether food is safe.

say: I'd accept **faster order lists** if dinner staffing stays paid.
I'd say **allergy pans** still need a cook's check.
think: One missing rota week eats **half my reserve** and leaves rent exposed.
I expect **cooking shifts** to continue through mild AI, though wages are tight.
do: Confirm **four weeks' shifts** and request written payday and overtime terms.
Check **AI order drafts** against stock, allergy labels and supplier sheets before buying food.
feel: I feel **anxious** about thin savings and late wages.
S0.quote: Two weeks' rent money can disappear in one bad rota.
fieldNote: Her **senior line skill** contrasts with below-market pay, two weeks saved and few nearby kitchens.
She **occasionally uses AI** for ordering drafts but checks stock and allergy labels herself.

steps.text: Confirm four weeks of paid line shifts and written payday/overtime terms
Check AI order drafts against stock, allergy labels and supplier sheets before purchase

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the owner a quicker order list is useful if the kitchen still gets staffed for the dinner rush. A screen cannot taste the sauce or clean the allergy pan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is already tight, and one lost rota week would eat half my reserve and leave little for rent. If AI stays small, I expect my cooking shifts to stay, but I still need the owner to pay them on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll confirm the next four weeks of paid line shifts and ask the owner to put payday and overtime terms in writing. In the first year of mild AI I'll keep cooking and check any AI order list against actual stock, allergy labels and the supplier sheet before anyone buys it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about ordinary late wages, not about a clever order list. Two weeks' rent money can disappear in one bad rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a stock list go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the supplier brought the wrong cream and I caught it against the allergy sheet before service. The owner paid for the replacement, but it delayed prep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the draft order food alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not let a draft list order food by itself. I check the labels and quantities against the boxes we actually have.

say: I'd ask whether **software rotas** reduce my paid lead hours.
I'd keep **allergen checks** with a named cook.
think: The **lead allowance** may shrink even while grill work stays.
A **smaller payslip** matters with only two weeks saved.
do: List **lead duties** and compare actual payslips this week.
Request **written cooking shifts** if software takes ordering; check allergens and temperatures before signing safety logs.
feel: I feel **anxious** about realistic pay loss despite a busy grill.
S1.quote: A full grill does not make a smaller payslip harmless.
fieldNote: Her **hands-on cooking** remains busy while software could reduce a variable lead allowance.
She **requires human checks** of allergen and temperature records before any safety sign-off.

steps.text: List lead duties and compare payslips this week
Request written cooking rota if software takes ordering; check allergens/temperatures before safety sign-off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner whether software doing orders and rotas will change my paid hours. I would insist the allergy check stays with a named cook, not a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering and rota notes take only a short part of my day, but they help justify my lead rate. If the owner removes that allowance while the grill stays busy, I could lose money I cannot spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll list the lead duties and compare them with my payslips. In the first year, if software takes the ordering slot, I'll ask for a written cooking rota and keep a human check of allergens and delivery temperatures; I won't accept an unpaid safety sign-off for a tool I did not inspect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the lead allowance could realistically shrink. A full grill does not make a smaller payslip harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is the lead allowance paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owner calls it a lead allowance, but it changes with the rota. I will ask for the actual amount in writing before arguing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks the safety log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The food-safety log stays on paper until the chef and I check the system against real thermometer readings. A wrong number on a screen can send someone to hospital.

say: I'd warn **2028 thinking AGI** may take ordering before 2031 cooking robots.
I'd ask for **guaranteed paid hours** on the kitchen line.
think: I expect **ordering allowance loss** by 2028, before physical cooking changes.
My **two-week cushion** makes even that smaller loss serious.
do: Request **written cooking hours**, allowance and paid season now.
Seek **posted paid hospital cook** after pay/hour cuts; require accepted certificate/experience, full weekly replacement net after fares and workable shift bus.
Keep **restaurant shifts** until signed offer; verify food-safety duties within competence and required second-cook allergy checks.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected allowance loss and few local openings.
S2.quote: A hospital kitchen has to advertise an actual opening.
fieldNote: Her **2028 ordering loss** precedes capable cooking robots around 2031.
A **hospital move** requires a posted qualified paid role, replacement net after bus fares, workable transport and a written offer.

steps.text: Request written cooking hours, allowance and paid season now
Seek posted paid hospital cooking after cuts; require certificate/experience, competent safety duties, full net-after-fares/bus
Keep restaurant shifts until written offer; check allergy labels/pan with required second cook

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that thinking AGI by 2028 could do the ordering and rota before a robot can cook around 2031. I would ask the owner which paid kitchen hours are guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the ordering allowance to disappear by 2028, but people will still handle hot food until the later robots arrive. Losing that small but real part of pay with two weeks saved makes another late wage dangerous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll ask for a written count of my cooking hours and allowance, request the next paid season and check a posted hospital-kitchen role only if it accepts my certificate and experience. In the first year after 2028 I'll keep the paid restaurant line while it exists; if hours or allowance fall, I'll apply only to a real paid vacancy with written net wages after bus fares replacing my full present weekly take-home, a workable bus home and food-safety duties I can perform, and stay until a suitable signed written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about an expected allowance loss and the small reserve. I can search. A hospital kitchen has to advertise an actual opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a hospital opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not seen a hospital vacancy this week. I would read its certificate and shift requirements before applying, not tell the owner I already have another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can AGI clear an allergy plate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, an ordering system cannot approve an allergy plate. I would read the ticket, clean the pan and check the ingredient label with another cook where our rules require it.

say: I'd demand **paid kitchen supervision** ahead of 2034 cooking robots.
I'd say **safe meals** need more than a machine menu.
think: Rota fees may **end before 2031** and later robots could reduce line hours.
I need **accepted training** with protected wages, not a rent-funded gamble.
do: Verify **actual posted paid supervisor** requirements and employer acceptance of cooking/advanced food-safety certificates before enrolling.
Enrol with **funded paid training** only if wages remain and bus works; practise allergen/hot-equipment checks under supervision.
Retain **paid line after 2031** until written offer; apply only if qualified and written replacement net after fares covers full weekly take-home.
feel: I feel **anxious** about pay and later line-hour risks despite preparation time.
S3.quote: I cannot pay for a course with rent money.
fieldNote: Her **advanced certificate plan** needs a posted accepting employer, funded paid hours and protected restaurant wages.
She **keeps supervised safety checks** and current pay until a qualified replacement job issues a written offer.

steps.text: Check any actual posted paid supervisor role accepts cooking/advanced food-safety certificates before enrolment
Enrol only with funded paid hours, preserved restaurant wages and workable bus; practise under supervision
Apply after 2031 to posted paid qualified role; require written full-weekly net-after-fares replacement
Stay until written offer; check allergens/hot equipment under experienced supervision

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the owner five years to thinking AGI by 2031 is time to price proper kitchen supervision before cooking robots around 2034. I would not call a machine-safe menu a safe meal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rota and ordering allowance may go before 2031, and a robot kitchen after 2034 could cut line hours. I could train for institutional food safety, but only if a real employer accepts the certificate and my wages stay paid while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'll ask the local training centre and hospital whether an actual paid kitchen-supervisor vacancy is posted and accepts my cooking certificate plus its advanced food-safety certificate. I'll enrol only with a funded place, paid training hours that preserve my restaurant wages and a bus that gets me home; in the first year after 2031 I'll keep my paid line, do supervised allergen and hot-equipment checks, and apply only if my credential qualifies and a written net wage after fares replaces my full present weekly take-home, staying until a signed written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the lead pay and later line hours, though five years gives me a route to check. I cannot pay for a course with rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the course funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre has not promised funding. If the hospital does not accept the certificate or paid time is unavailable, I will keep the line and not enrol on credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who signs off a safe meal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hospital cook must know which pan and ingredient went into a patient's meal. I would practise under an experienced supervisor and never approve a hot machine for use or release an allergy meal alone before sign-off.

say: I'd demand **real wages** and safe training before 2039 cooking robots.
I'd say **today's rent** matters through a long countdown.
think: At **37**, I still need paid kitchen work, even if robots change how orders are cooked.
My **two-week reserve** today cannot live on a promised decade.
do: Request **twelve months' paid rota** and save cleared overtime after rent, food and bus fares toward one month.
Keep **qualified paid kitchen/supervisor hours** after 2036 with human checks of hot equipment and allergens.
Seek **posted kitchen work** only with qualification, written replacement net after travel, workable route and offer before leaving.
feel: I feel **anxious** about current low pay and thin savings despite the longer runway.
S4.quote: A longer calendar will not pay this month's rent.
fieldNote: Her **one-month savings goal** relies only on overtime actually paid after essentials, not current rent money.
She **stays in paid kitchens** through 2036 only with safe human checks and a qualifying written replacement offer for any move.

steps.text: Request written twelve-month paid kitchen rota and save cleared overtime after essentials toward one month
Keep qualified paid post-2036 kitchen hours with human allergen and hot-equipment checks
Seek posted kitchen role only with qualifications, written replacement net after travel and workable route
Stay at restaurant until suitable written offer before moving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friends ten years to thinking AGI by 2036 lets me insist on real wages and safe kitchen training before cooking robots arrive around 2039. A longer calendar will not pay this month's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I should still have years of work ahead. If restaurant cooking remains paid, I may stay, but two weeks saved today makes a decade of promises less useful than a written rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request twelve months of paid kitchen shifts and set aside any overtime actually paid after rent, food and bus fares toward one month of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid kitchen or supervisor hours I am qualified and trained to do, check hot equipment and allergens with a human lead, and consider another kitchen only with a real vacancy, written net wage after travel replacing my full present weekly restaurant take-home, a workable route and a signed written offer before I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the thin reserve and low pay today, despite more years to prepare. I would feel better after one month of expenses is actually in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no overtime is paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there is no overtime, I save nothing from that source. I would not take rent money to make a target look complete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave cooking at 37?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I am not retiring at 37. I would need paid hours and safe equipment whether the kitchen uses a robot or a wooden spoon.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the ordering allowance could vanish before I have even a month's reserve, and cooking robots could follow in 2031. Written paid hours, a real hospital posting that accepts my certificate, and a bus home after a replacement shift would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs the allergy ticket when a new system makes the order. A cook can be replaced on a rota faster than a wrong plate can be recalled.

headlineQuote: A cook can be replaced on a rota faster than a wrong plate can be recalled.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old lead cook** with a vocational certificate, rented room and no children.
Her **below-market pay**, two-week reserve and few nearby kitchens make even lost lead allowance serious.
She **sometimes uses AI** for order drafts but keeps allergen and equipment checks in human hands.
She checks **funded paid training** and qualifying posted hospital work before changing kitchens.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase Esther's ordering allowance before 2031 cooking robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid shifts**, an actual accepting hospital vacancy and replacement wages after bus fares would help.
